newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-NAMES START TO CHANGE IN POST-APARTHEID ERA.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-NAMES START TO CHANGE IN POST-APARTHEID ERA.

text.p: Old names from South Africa's apartheid era are changing as provincial rugby sides slowly come to terms with Nelson Mandela's republic.

While the South African Rugby Football Union (SARFU) is beset by scandals and rumours of financial misdealings, nepotism and racism, the provinces are formally acknowledging the changes Mandela has wrought by adopting new names.

In late 1994 the old apartheid administrative region of Transvaal was reborn as Gauteng, meaning place of gold. But it is only recently that the five rugby unions still carrying Transvaal in their names have begun casting off the past.

South Eastern Transvaal's rugby authority has embraced the region's administrative name to become Mpumalanga and Eastern Transvaal will definitely change their name, probably to the Red Devils, after their golden jubilee celebrations in May.
The 59-year-old Northern Transvaal rugby union will discuss becoming the Blue Bulls later in March and Western Transvaal are likely to become North West at an April executive meeting.
But the most significant change will be Transvaal's at its annual meeting on March 17.
After 108 years, the Transvaal Rugby Union -- the Johannesburg fiefdom of SARFU president Louis Luyt -- will become the Golden Lions Rugby Union.
"In the spirit of reconciliation and in the spirit of Gauteng we are very happy to be known now as the Golden Lions Rugby Union," said chief executive Johan Prinsloo.
"Transvaal as a region is no more."
The Transvaal executive approved the name change without a murmur of dissent and elsewhere the change has also been made seamlessly.
"I put it to all our clubs at a meeting and there wasn't one dissenting voice. They all said 'go for it'," said Willem Strauss, chief executive of Mpumalanga's rugby administration.

"We wanted the people of the province to identify with us. It was also a marketing decision. Our sponsors would say to us 'where is South Eastern Transvaal?' There isn't that problem with Mpumalanga," Strauss said.

The region, home to the country's premier game reserves including the famed Kruger park, is running a newspaper contest to choose a nickname. Strauss favours the Mpumalanga Falcons or Mpumalanga Eagles.
For once rugby, widely seen as the bastion of white Afrikaners, appears to have stolen a march on cricket, regarded as the blueprint for successful integration.
While their Western Transvaal has become North West and Eastern Transvaal has become Easterns, both Northern Transvaal and Transvaal are still to make the change.
"The names of some of the provinces represent the past and not the future," acknowledged United Cricket Board managing director Ali Bacher.
"This is a decision that we leave to the provinces, but from a personal point of view I would encourage them to change their names."
One emblem of the old South Africa that will not change is the Springbok.
Rugby fought to retain the emblem a year ago, and received Mandela's seal of approval, although cricket voluntarily replaced the South African gazelle with a flower, the king protea.
Significantly, the black press chose to rename the Springbok rugby team, christening it Amabokoboko ("our boks") during a wave of national affection during the successful 1995 World Cup.
The enthusiasm turned to anger last month when a taped recording of an ugly racist tirade from Springbok coach Andre Markgraaff was aired. A tearful Markgraaff resigned.
